title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
description: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, accord
body: Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made.But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met, and that the dignity and safety of the trans patient and of other patients are maintained.Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman. The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward. The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentus shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied. "NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients."This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected. The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it."The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said. "Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces. Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms. She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation. An appeal is under way and expected to reach the courts next year.

schema.headline: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says

title: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel has said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her in a hotel has said she was left feeling "dirty" and afraid she may be pregnant in the aftermath of the alleged attack.The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.Video evidence played to the jury at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday showed one of his complainants tell the police: "He raped me basically and I know that happened."The jury heard one of Brand's accusers say she had met him in 1999, before he was famous.The woman was heard speaking in a police interview recorded in 2023, when reporting the alleged crime.She said she had attended the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth and went to a fringe event where she said she spoke to Brand. She alleges he later raped her.The complainant said they had both gone back to a hotel room. She told the officer she thought Brand "was gay" when they met earlier and she didn't feel like he was "trying it on with her".She said she had been in the bathroom, but when she came out "he had like briefs on - and I was like taken aback and shocked. He was prancing around".The complainant alleged Brand told her: "Don't worry, that's how I am".She recalled thinking "what on earth have I got into" when, she claims, a shirtless Brand made her take photos of him before the alleged attack.She told the officer: "I'm reporting that Russell Brand did rape me."What I'm going to say now - then, I second guessed myself if it was rape because it was so normal."Sorry... he raped me basically - I know that happened. I remember him touching my breasts a lot - while kissing my neck."The woman recounted how Brand acted "like Basil Fawlty when he does his goose steps" before the alleged rape.She told the officer: "I remember him being like an ostrich - like a bird because he was very leggy."I wasn't laughing, I just remember him jumping up and down being silly."The woman said after Brand left the room she was "just sitting there crying and I felt stupid," adding: "In that moment in time I was just shocked."At one point in the police interview, she cried while saying "this was something dirty that had happened".She said she "thought it was my fault", adding that she was "having nightmares" about the possibility of being pregnant.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accuser says alleged rape left her afraid she may be pregnant

title: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport
description: A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.Customs officials said t
body: A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport. They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase.They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks. "My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office.Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul.The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance. He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul.As for the surviving animals, they are  being looked after at a snake farm in Germany."Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said. Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport.They were destined for private buyers in Germany.

schema.headline: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
description: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previo
body: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die"."I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.  The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.

schema.headline: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad

title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
description: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.Ukra
body: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery after Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.Ukraine's president said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and he said curbs on Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.Ukrainian defence sources told the BBC some Starlink functionality had resumed as of Thursday morning.They said its military service Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, although it remains unclear whether the restrictions to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake"."Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."He added: "Peace will be achieved when [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.The Ukrainian president told the FT he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

schema.headline: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume

title: Newspaper headlines: GPs 'standstill' and 'silver for Peaty'
description: The Daily Telegraph says the chancellor will announce that Ministry of Defence sites, unused NHS property and Network Rail land could be sold to help
body: The Daily Telegraph says the chancellor will announce that Ministry of Defence sites, unused NHS property and Network Rail land could be sold to help fill a black hole in the public finances, external.  It reports there will be a ban on non-essential consultants. The Times says selling surplus public property was a policy championed by former Conservative Chancellor George Osborne, external and the paper suggests Rachel Reeves will echo his arguments for austerity. However, a Treasury source tells the Guardian that this is not about a "return to austerity", external, but repairing what they describe as the damage from "14 years of unfunded promises".The Financial Times stresses that the Treasury has not rejected speculation that the chancellor's statement is a "softening up exercise for tax rises in the autumn".  Writing in the Daily Express, shadow chancellor Jeremy Hunt accuses Labour of trying to "fabricate their own truth", external to justify tax increases. He suggests Ms Reeves has her eyes firmly set on capital gains tax, inheritance tax and even pensions relief. In its editorial, the Daily Mail says that were the government to slash infrastructure projects and increase wealth taxes, it would "snuff out" growth "in a heartbeat", external.Both the Daily Mail and the i lead on the threat that GPs could bring "the NHS to a standstill" if they vote to take industrial action for the first time in 60 years. The ballot closes at midday. The Daily Mail says if the action goes ahead it is feared up to three million GP appointments could disappear, external every month. The Daily Mirror says underfunding general practice could lead to a two-tier system where some patients go private. The Department of Health tells the i it is planning for all contingencies, external.The Guardian and the Times both focus on US efforts to urge Israel to exercise restraint after the rocket attack which killed 12 children and teenagers in the occupied Golan Heights. The Daily Telegraph notes in its leader column that Hezbollah is "an altogether different challenge to Hamas", external. The prospect of a war spreading across the Middle East will alarm foreign governments which, the paper says, have turned a "blind eye" to the threat from Hezbollah for too long.On its front page, the Financial Times says the US Vice-President Kamala Harris has raised $200m in the first week of her election campaign. The paper says that is more than either President Joe Biden or Donald Trump collected in the whole of June. The FT says there are signs in the polls that the vice-president is closing the gap between her and Mr Trump.The Olympic swimmer, Adam Peaty, is pictured on many front pages after being pipped to first place last night by two one-hundredths of a second.  Most papers choose a photo in which he is smiling, holding up his silver medal. The Sun says he missed out on gold "by a fingernail" while the Times highlights his post-race comment that he was "crying happy tears", external.  The Mirror sums up its disappointment with a pun on his name, "what a Peaty".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: GPs 'standstill' and 'silver for Peaty'

title: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses
description: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital
body: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition.Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC.The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris.Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes".Warning: This article contains distressing detailsAn English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said."I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away.""There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels".The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down.There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.

schema.headline: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses

title: Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK
description: Figure caption, Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK returnByNoor NanjiRoyal correspondent and Daniela RelphSenior Royal corresp
body: Figure caption, Watch: Harry and Meghan at first joint engagement since UK returnByNoor NanjiRoyal correspondent and Daniela RelphSenior Royal correspondentUpdated 3 hours agoThe Duchess of Sussex has made her first official public appearance since moving back to the UK, telling well-wishers "it's great to be back".Meghan arrived at a youth charity in Nottingham alongside her husband, the Duke of Sussex, on Thursday morning. The pair, who are also expected to visit a food bank later, hugged and posed for selfies with the public.The duchess spoke to a number of people in the crowd, telling one "we got lucky" as they chatted about the weather.She has shared glimpses of her life back in the UK on social media, but this is the first time she has attended any public events since the family returned from California.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Meghan clutched some flowers and some friendship bracelets she was handedDuring a bracelet-making workshop, Meghan disclosed her daughter Princess Lilibet had been enjoying a new hobby.When one youngster told the duchess she liked doing gymnastics, Meghan replied: "Oh yeah. Our daughter is doing that too right now. She loves it."Later, she gave the young girls some advice on building confidence."We have to remember to talk to ourselves like we talk to our best friends," she said. "It's really important to be just as kind to yourself."A spokesperson for Harry and Meghan said Nottingham is "a special place" for them both, as it is where they made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.The pair are attending these events not as working royals, but as public figures and supporters of the projects they're visiting.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The duchess joined in with a friendship bracelet making session in the centreThe Royal Household has made it clear they view them as private citizens.Despite that, Thursday’s schedule has a distinctly royal feel to it.The first stop on their visit to Nottingham is the Community Recording Studio, a charity which Prince Harry has been supporting since 2013.Its CEO Trevor Rose told the BBC they only found out about the trip a few weeks ago, and could not believe it."It's exciting times. Completely random, phoned, mentioned a idea, said they'd like to come down," he said."I thought it was going to be something in the future, next thing I know it's two weeks later and we are here, so yeah it's a complete shock."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The duke and duchess helped prepare food in the Himmah Hub on Thursday afternoonLater in the day the pair visited Himmah Hub, a local charity tackling food poverty.They watched cooking classes taking place and helped prepare food parcels, donning chef's aprons to help with the prep themselves.During the visit, Meghan and Harry kissed, hugged and held hands with their Grenfell "ladies", who featured in a community cookbook championed by Meghan.The women who cooked for the Grenfell families in the wake of the fatal tower block fire received regular private visits from the duchess, who later said that catching up with the community cooks was "really, really meaningful".Their third engagement is at Epic Partners, a group working to support young people through youth work, sport and mentoring.The couple have a private security team with them in Nottingham and local police teams are understood to be aware of their visit.Harry and Meghan's spokesperson told BBC News they were "really excited" to be back together in Nottingham, nine years since their last joint visit.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Duke and Duchess beamed as they greeted the public in Nottingham on Thursday"They are back here primarily because they support and believe in the organisations they are visiting."They enjoy coming back to revisit projects they are personally invested in, to meet the same people and understand what is happening and how things are changing."In 2017, Harry and Meghan visited Nottingham's Lace Market before a visit to a World Aids Day charity fair.Pictures from that trip showed the couple smiling as they met enthusiastic crowds.The pair and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, returned to the UK in August after living in the US for six years.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The royal couple shared a laugh as they took their seats inside the centreThey have reportedly settled in the Cotswolds, and their children have moved schools after issues were raised by their security team about the school run.It also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is reconsidering Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.The Sussexes will not be spending Christmas with the King at the traditional royal family gathering at Sandringham, Norfolk. BBC News understands that they are likely to spend it privately with Meghan's mother Doria Ragland.

schema.headline: Meghan makes first official public appearance since moving back to UK

title: Another man admits raping woman drugged and abused by husband
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The victim looked on from the public gallery as Graham Brougham, 74, changed his plea to guiltyByJonny HumphriesRe
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The victim looked on from the public gallery as Graham Brougham, 74, changed his plea to guiltyByJonny HumphriesReporting fromat Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court and Rachael LazaroNorth WestUpdated 1 hour agoAnother man has pleaded guilty to raping a woman who was drugged and abused by her husband without her knowledge for over 20 years.Graham Brougham, 74, is the oldest of 13 men who were charged with sexual offences against the victim after being allegedly invited into her home, in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, to abuse her by her husband.The husband, in his sixties, has already admitted 62 offences against his wife - including rape - and has given a witness statement detailing "what he says happened".Brougham, from Northwich, was told by a judge at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court that he "should be under no illusion his sentence will be custody and a long time in custody."The victim, who held hands with a family member, watched on from the public gallery as Brougham answered "guilty" in the dock to a charge of raping her in September 2024.Image caption, Graham Brougham leaving court after admitting his guiltThe husband, who remains in custody, cannot be identified to protect the anonymity of his wife.Two other men, 59-year-old Keith Fotheringham from Dundee, Scotland; and Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport, had already admitted sexually abusing her at previous hearings.The trial of 10 other defendants accused of sexual offences against the victim has been delayed until 2 November for legal and practical reasons.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sean Peers, 38, changed his plea to guilty and admitted sexually assaulting the woman earlier this monthThey are all alleged to have committed offences against the same victim between 2015 and November 2025.Brougham was released on conditional bail and will be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial of his co-defendants.Earlier this month, the nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, were told that the husband had provided a witness statement detailing "what it is he says happened" after his guilty pleas.Judge Maurice Greene said: "That statement is a long statement and that has been disclosed to all defence counsel and it contains a lot of detail."Image caption, Alan Keelan, Jonathan Kirk and Jordan Wallace deny the charges against them and, along with seven others, will go on trial next monthThe judge said the statement contained "lots of pages and lots of documents" and that lawyers in the case were "going through it carefully", which was ongoing work.The other defendants are:Philip Wild, 58, from StockportJordan Wallace, 31, from ManchesterAlan Keelan, 42, from ManchesterJonathan Kirk, 43, from StockportRobert Stewart, 70, from StockportMohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abodeRichard Townsend, 37, from RochdaleKarl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, from SomersetDaniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable, KentDavid Graves, 59, from Ilkeston, DerbyshireThe trial continues.

schema.headline: Another man admits raping woman drugged and abused by husband

title: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?
description: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!",
body: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines."Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says."And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust.He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein."If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded.Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away."The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more
description: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he rele
body: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all of the documents and answers key questions.The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced."One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers  from FFE," Hewitt said."I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing."I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them."It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize."The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate."That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change."Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology."Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added."What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released. Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened.  "Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said.Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023."I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added."We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel."This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms."Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues".Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed.BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat.Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card."What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt."Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room."The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed."When he puts other dignitaries in front of his 211 associations, then he's lost what football is about," Hewitt said."And that was said by a number of people, not just the Europeans."How the Peace Prize came to be awarded will be the subject of an investigation by the Fifa social committee."They will consider, first of all, how the Peace Prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed," Hewitt said."That committee will report back to Council in December and then Council will make the decision based on its recommendation."Today there was a watershed moment where it's very clear in order to move forward, which we all want to do, we have to understand the past."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more

title: Severe drought declared in parts of southern England
description: South East Water's operations director Douglas Whitfield said standpipes remained part of the company's drought plan but were unlikely to be needed.Wh
body: South East Water's operations director Douglas Whitfield said standpipes remained part of the company's drought plan but were unlikely to be needed.Whitfield said a wet winter had been forecast but timings were not clear and the firm was making any adjustments it could to protect supplies.Whitfield said South East Water, which supplies more than two million customers, said 92 repair crews were out across Sussex and Kent tackling leaks to minimise loss from the network.In an email sent to customers South East Water said it was optimising water pressure across the county and had more than doubled the number of teams tackling leaks in the region, increasing from seven to 16.It said the number of leaks in the affected area had fallen from 181 to 97 and that more than 1,300 leaks had been repaired since 1 April.Wessex Water, which supplies customers from Wimbleball, introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years in August and said the restrictions would remain in place for the foreseeable future.The water company said it had increased leak repairs, moved water into the area from more resilient sources and adjusted water pressure in some communities to conserve supplies and urged customers to continue using water carefully.Will Willoughby, director of water supply at Wessex Water, said: "We saw record levels of demand through the network - and it sustained above the 400 million litres a day for 48 days, which is far and away the toughest year that we've seen in terms of that height in demand."He said customer impact "should be none" but encouraged customers to continue to be mindful about water usage.Paul Tompkins, deputy president of The National Farmers' Union (NFU) said it had been a "torrid year for farmers", where the conditions proved "very difficult" to harvest crops, provide water for livestock, and a "potential dry winter could have implications for next year's crops". title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
description: The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called  a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.Healey told the BBC "i
body: The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called  a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will". But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending". The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August. "It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register". He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate"."The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet."Healey went on to say the Budget would be tough and not include inflation top-ups for public sector pay.Some experts and unions have called for extra cash for some departmental budgets, to account for the rising costs of providing public services and pay.But, asked whether there would be extra money made available for nurses and doctors, the chancellor said: "People recognise these times that are tough for everyone, and what they do expect of a government is to manage with the budgets we've got, deliver the public services they need, and that's the challenge."Our departments have their spending, and the prime minister and I, being in lockstep about this, where we want to do things, we have to make sure that we can pay for them within the budgets that we've got and control spending."

schema.headline: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget

title: William Chapman died from 'multiple traumatic injuries' in tiger attack, inquest hears
description: Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining mult
body: Brookes told the hearing: "He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death."Park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended but confirmed his death at the scene.The senior coroner said her office was awaiting a more substantial report as to the extent of his injuries. South Yorkshire Police provided a number of witness statements from the public and staff who were at the wildlife park at the time, the hearing was told.Mundy instructed staff to contact Yorkshire Wildlife Park to ask them to keep any relevant CCTV and inform the coroner of any previous visits by Chapman to the park.After opening the inquest, which Chapman's family chose not to attend, on Thursday morning, Mundy adjourned proceedings until 18 March 2027.Speaking after the hearing, a neighbour of Chapman told the BBC he was "very polite and well-spoken" and a "lovely man".Josh, 24, who lived in the same building as Chapman, said: "He'd always have a laugh and a joke. He was quite well kept, he'd look after himself physically. He loved his F1, he'd talk for hours about his F1 if he could."Discussing the online comments and speculation in the aftermath of the incident, he said: "People didn't know him. If you don't know him, don't make a comment."The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation of the Yorkshire Wildlife Park.An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.What we know about wildlife park tiger attackMobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.The park would reopen on Friday for the first time since the fatal incident, a spokesperson confirmed.In a statement, they said that staff members' "heartfelt sympathies" remained with Chapman's family and loved ones. "The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff team and animals remain our highest priority," they added."As we welcome visitors back, we would ask everyone to be understanding and respectful towards our staff team, who have shown tremendous professionalism and dedication during an exceptionally difficult time. "We are providing specialist trauma support and ongoing care for those affected."We continue to assist South Yorkshire Police and other relevant agencies with their ongoing inquiries into the circumstances of this tragic incident."A park spokesperson previously said the rare Amur tiger involved, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.A health and safety investigation has also been launched by City of Doncaster Council.

title: King Charles praises Welsh 'sense of belonging' as he opens Senedd
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The King said he was proud of his "special connection with Wales"ByDavid DeansWales political reporter and Ad
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The King said he was proud of his "special connection with Wales"ByDavid DeansWales political reporter and Adrian BrowneWales political reporterUpdated 2 hours agoKing Charles III has praised Welsh people's "sense of belonging", as he and Queen Camilla officially opened the Senedd's seventh term.The visit marked the King's first official meeting with First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth following the election victory of Plaid Cymru - a party rooted in a strong republican tradition.In his speech to the Senedd, with most of its 96 members in attendance including opposition parties Reform, Labour and the Tories, the King also expressed concern for the impact of climate change on the Welsh countryside. About 30 protesters by the steps of the Senedd were vocal throughout the royal visit, and one was arrested on suspicion of breaching the Public Order Act.Chants of "not my King" and "down, down, down with the crown" could be heard from protesters during the visit.Wales' national poet did not take part in the ceremony as had been planned, after Senedd officials rejected the poem she had written for the event and cancelled her performance.The King used his visit to the Senedd to say he would return to Wales next week to visit Aberfan, scene of the 1966 coal tip disaster, and met a survivor who had been pulled from the rubble aged six.A 21-gun salute in Cardiff Bay marked the King's arrival in the city, and Plaid leader ap Iorwerth greeted the King on the Senedd steps, together with the Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies and the Labour Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, who represented the UK government.Image source, Senedd CymruImage caption, The King praised the "connection between place, people, culture and belonging" found in WalesAddressing the Senedd chamber, the King said he had "always felt immensely privileged and proud to have had such a special connection with Wales, with its language, its culture and its landscape for so much of my life"."The character and identity of Wales have always been built from the strength of its places, and the relationships of trust, service and neighbourliness found within them - that distinctively Welsh idea of connection, the profound connection between place, people, culture and belonging," he said."As you take forward your task of government, we know you will bear always in mind, and draw inspiration from, those shared strengths, as you work on behalf of the people of this most special corner of the Earth." The King then expressed concern about the impact of climate change, following a number of wildfires this summer that blighted parts of Wales.He said: "No-one can have failed to have been struck by the way the very colours of our countryside changed during this summer's heatwaves. "Nor could they have failed to be deeply concerned at what this means for our rapidly changing planet."I am sure we all share that most profound concern for the environment of this country entrusted to our care."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, It was the King's first official meeting with Rhun ap Iorwerth since he became Wales' first ministerAp Iorwerth said the ceremony marked a "new chapter" for national democracy and that it was a Senedd opening "unlike any that has gone before it".The Senedd expanded to 96 members for May's elections, which represented a "significant moment in the continued evolution of Welsh democracy," said the first minister.He said the parliament was "strengthened in its capacity to scrutinise" as a result of the change.Buckingham Palace said the King also held an audience with the first minister at the nearby Millennium Centre. Irranca-Davies said his message for new Senedd members, elected in May, was that the "institution is at its best when we recognise that disagreement need not mean division"."We will disagree, we should disagree, vigorous debate is part of a healthy democracy," he said."But we should never lose sight of what brings every one of us here: a shared responsibility to serve the people of Wales," he added.Elizabeth II had opened every previous session of the Senedd before her death four years ago, her last one being 2021 when she had been joined by the current King and Queen.Image caption, "I'm disappointed more than anything," Hanan Issa, the National Poet of Wales, told BBC WalesBriefings to the media before the event had said a poetry reading would be made by the National Poet of Wales, Hanan Issa, at the ceremony.On Wednesday, Issa posted to Instagram saying To Grow, the poem they submitted, was rejected on the grounds that the ceremony was "apolitical".Among other issues, the poem referred to Gaza and trans healthcare, and Issa said a second version that used "more abstract language" was also rejected.Issa said she had received a brief to "celebrate" Members of the Senedd (MSs) and their "achievements in being elected, while serving as a reminder of their commitment to the people of Wales"."I'm disappointed more than anything. This is the chamber where political discussion is had, and this very much says that political discussion framed as a poem is not welcome," Issa added.The Senedd commission said: "After a development process, we concluded that the poem was not the right fit for this occasion."It added: "We respect the National Poet of Wales' artistic independence and continue to admire and value their work."Image caption, Aberfan disaster survivor Gareth Jones showed the King a photograph of his father meeting him and his sister on the day after the tragedyThe King and Queen, along with the Prince of Wales, will return to south Wales next week to pay their respects at the Aberfan memorial garden exactly 60 years since the disaster.The incident saw a junior school and surrounding houses in the village engulfed in coal slurry after a colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.Gareth Jones, now 67, said he had joined Thursday's ceremony in the Senedd to show the King a photograph of his father meeting him and his sister on the day after the tragedy.Figure caption, The Senedd building was officially opened in 2006 by the late queen - who had also opened every previous Welsh Parliament and Welsh assembly term since 1999The meeting with the leader of Plaid Cymru - a pro-independence party rooted in a strong republican tradition - marked a significant and symbolic moment.Ap Iorwerth's Plaid Cymru took control of the Welsh government following May's Senedd election, replacing Labour who had led every previous government since devolution in 1999. The Plaid leader told an interview with Politics Home last year that he did not believe in "kings and princes", but said the issue was not a "political priority for him".He said he appreciated the monarchy remained "important" to many in Wales, but said there was a "clear argument to be made that the Prince of Wales title should be consigned to the history books".What is an official opening of the Senedd?Held after an election takes place, the opening ceremony formally marks a new Senedd term.The head of state attends in recognition of the Senedd's role in Welsh public life.The late queen opened the first National Assembly for Wales - the previous incarnation of the Senedd - in 1999, and every post-election session until 2022.The mace is a ceremonial staff used at formal parliamentary events.It was gifted by the Australian New South Wales parliament for the building's opening in 2006, handcrafted from gold, silver and brass.The Senedd building is 20 years old this year, having opened its doors in 2006. It expanded from 60 to 96 members at the May election.

schema.headline: King Charles praises Welsh 'sense of belonging' as he opens Senedd
